lines.s: Welcome back to Mind Matters. Today we're asking: how quickly do we judge people? With me is psychologist Dr Lina Haddad.
Thanks for having me. The short answer is: incredibly quickly. Researchers at Princeton found that we form an impression of a face in about a tenth of a second.
A tenth of a second? That's faster than a blink!
Exactly. And giving people more time doesn't change their judgement much; it just makes them more confident about it.
So what are we actually judging?
Mainly two things: whether someone seems trustworthy and whether they seem competent. Facial expression, posture and tone of voice matter more than the words people say.
That's a little worrying. Can we change a bad first impression?
Yes, but it takes time. Studies suggest you need several positive meetings to change one negative impression. So it's worth making a good one from the start.
Any quick tips?
Smile naturally, make eye contact, and show genuine interest in the other person. People remember how you made them feel.

reading.text: For centuries, people have tried to describe personality. Ancient doctors believed that our temperament depended on four body fluids, while modern psychologists prefer to measure it. Today, the most widely accepted model is known as the "Big Five". It suggests that almost every personality can be described using five broad dimensions. The first is openness: open people tend to be curious and creative, and they enjoy new experiences. The second, conscientiousness, describes how organised and reliable someone is; conscientious people are often meticulous and rarely miss deadlines. The third is extraversion, which measures how much energy we get from being with others. The fourth, agreeableness, refers to how compassionate and cooperative we are. Finally, neuroticism describes how easily we experience negative emotions such as worry or anger. Importantly, these are not boxes. Each trait is a scale, and most people fall somewhere in the middle. Psychologists usually measure them with a questionnaire of statements such as "I pay attention to details" or "I start conversations easily", which people rate from one to five. Someone might be highly conscientious at work but fairly relaxed at home. Research also suggests that personality is not completely fixed. Many people become more conscientious and agreeable as they get older, and major life events can shift our traits too. Critics argue that five dimensions cannot capture the full complexity of a human being, and they have a point: the model says little about our values, beliefs or sense of humour. However, the model has proved surprisingly useful. It can predict, to some extent, how well people perform at work, how satisfied they are in relationships, and even how healthy they are. Perhaps its greatest value is that it encourages self-awareness. Knowing where you are on each scale will not change who you are, but it may help you understand why you react the way you do.

lines.s: In today's episode, we're talking about grandparents. My guest, Professor Omar Saleh, studies family relationships. Welcome!
Thank you. It's a topic close to my heart. I was brought up partly by my grandmother.
Lucky you! So, what does the research say?
A well-known study from the University of Oxford found that children whose grandparents were closely involved in their lives had fewer emotional and behavioural problems.
Why do you think that is?
Grandparents often have more patience and more time than busy parents. They tend to listen without judging, so children confide in them.
Is it good for the grandparents too?
Absolutely. Older people who spend time with their grandchildren often feel less lonely and more active. It's a two-way benefit.
But in many cities, families now live far apart.
True. That's why video calls, even short ones, can make a real difference. The important thing is regular contact.

reading.en: Does Birth Order Shape Who We Are?
reading.text: Ask any family with several children and you will probably hear the same stories. The firstborn is responsible and bossy, the youngest is charming and spoiled, and the middle child is always complaining that nobody notices them. The idea that birth order shapes personality was made popular almost a hundred years ago by the Austrian psychologist Alfred Adler, who was himself a second child. According to his theory, older children receive their parents' full attention until a sibling arrives, which pushes them to work hard to stay important. Younger children, on the other hand, have to find different ways to stand out, so they may become more rebellious or creative. Adler even suggested that only children, who never have to share their parents, might find it harder to cooperate with others. It is an attractive theory, and it seems to match our everyday experience. However, when researchers have tested it scientifically, the results have been surprisingly weak. In 2015, a team of psychologists analysed data from more than 20,000 people in Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States. They compared brothers and sisters from the same families and found no meaningful link between birth order and traits such as extraversion, emotional stability or agreeableness. The only consistent difference was a very small advantage in intelligence test scores for older siblings, too small to notice in daily life. So why do the stereotypes survive? Part of the answer may be that we compare siblings at different ages. A ten-year-old naturally seems more responsible than a six-year-old, but that is because of age, not birth order. Our expectations may also influence how we treat children, which in turn affects how they behave. In the end, it seems that parenting, friendships and life experiences matter far more than whether you were born first or last. So next time someone blames your personality on being the eldest, you can tell them that the science disagrees.

And what changed?
My youngest daughter finished university, and she said, "Dad, it's your turn." I enrolled the following month as a mature student.

reading.en: Why We Forget, and How to Remember
reading.text: In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus performed a strange experiment on himself. He memorised long lists of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF", and then tested how many he could remember after different periods of time. The results were depressing. Within twenty minutes, he had forgotten almost half of what he had learnt, and after a day, he had lost around two thirds. He called this pattern the "forgetting curve". Fortunately, Ebbinghaus also discovered how to fight it. Every time he reviewed a list, the curve became flatter, which meant that he forgot more slowly. This is known as the spacing effect: information that is reviewed several times over days or weeks is retained far longer than information that is crammed in one night. More recent research has added a second powerful idea: the testing effect. When students try to recall information from memory, for example by answering questions or explaining a topic to a friend, they remember it much better than when they simply reread their notes. Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as understanding. Psychologists call this an "illusion of competence". So what does this mean for learners? First, study in short sessions spread over time rather than in one long session. Second, close the book and test yourself regularly, even if you make mistakes; struggling to remember is a sign that your brain is working hard. Third, mix different topics instead of practising one thing at a time. This feels harder, but it helps the brain to see connections. None of these techniques is new; Ebbinghaus could have told us most of them over a century ago. The challenge is not knowing them, but having the discipline to use them.

dialogue.en: The Rise of the Side Hustle

lines.s: Welcome to Work Talk. Today: side hustles. My guest, Noor Hassan, is a career coach. Noor, what exactly is a side hustle?
It's any work you do outside your main job to earn extra money or follow a passion. It might be tutoring, selling crafts online or freelancing as a designer.
Why are they becoming so popular?

Partly because of the cost of living. Many people have been struggling to make ends meet on one salary. But technology has also made it easier. You can open an online shop from your phone in ten minutes.
Is it all about money?
Not at all. In my experience, about half of my clients start a side hustle because they want more job satisfaction. Their main job pays the bills, but the side hustle is where they feel creative.
Are there any risks?
Burnout is the big one. If you've been working eight hours and then you work another four every evening, something has to give. I always tell people: protect your sleep and set clear limits.
And can a side hustle become a full-time job?
Definitely. Some of my clients had been running their side business for two or three years before they felt confident enough to leave their jobs.

reading.text: Every major new technology has been accompanied by fear about jobs. In the early nineteenth century, English textile workers known as the Luddites smashed the machines that they believed would destroy their livelihoods. A century later, people worried that cars would put coachmen out of work, which they did. Yet, in the long run, these technologies created far more jobs than they destroyed. Today, artificial intelligence is causing similar anxiety, but there is an important difference. Previous waves of automation mainly replaced blue-collar work, such as lifting, weaving or assembling. AI, on the other hand, is increasingly able to perform white-collar tasks: writing reports, analysing data, translating documents and even writing code. For the first time, office workers are wondering whether their jobs are safe. Economists are divided. Some predict large-scale redundancies in areas such as customer service and administration. Others argue that AI will mostly change jobs rather than eliminate them, taking over repetitive tasks and leaving humans free to focus on work that requires judgement, creativity and empathy. A doctor who uses AI to read scans, for instance, may have more time to talk to patients. What seems clear is that the skills employers value are shifting. Technical knowledge goes out of date quickly, so the ability to learn new tools may matter more than any particular qualification. Communication, collaboration and critical thinking, which machines still find difficult, are likely to become even more important. Perhaps the most useful question, then, is not "Will AI take my job?" but "How can I work alongside it?" Workers who have been upskilling and experimenting with these tools are already finding that they can be more productive, not less. As a popular saying in the tech world puts it, AI will not replace you, but a person using AI might.

lines.s: Can money buy happiness? That's today's big question. I'm joined by economist Dr Rana Jaber. Rana, welcome.
Thank you. It's a question people have been asking for centuries!
So, what does the research say?
For a long time, the famous answer was that happiness rises with income, but only up to about 75,000 dollars a year in the United States. After that, it seemed to level off.
Seemed?
Yes. A larger study in 2021 found that, for most people, happiness kept rising with income. So money does help, especially when it removes stress about bills and debts.
Is there a "right" way to spend money?

Interestingly, yes. People tend to get more lasting happiness from experiences, like travel or a meal with friends, than from objects. And spending money on other people makes us happier than spending it on ourselves.
So my advice to listeners should be…?
Save for a rainy day, avoid debt, and if you have some disposable income, buy memories, not things.

reading.text: Long before coins or banknotes existed, people in Mesopotamia had already developed one of the world's first financial systems. Around 5,000 years ago, temples and palaces in cities like Uruk stored grain and silver, and scribes recorded loans on clay tablets. A farmer might borrow barley in spring and promise to repay it, with interest, after the harvest. In fact, some of the earliest examples of writing are not poems or stories but records of who owed what to whom. Silver, measured by weight in a unit called the shekel, gradually became a common way to measure value. The Code of Hammurabi, written in Babylon nearly 4,000 years ago, even set rules about maximum interest rates and debts. True coins appeared much later, in the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, around the seventh century BC. Because each coin had a standard weight and was stamped by the king, people no longer had to weigh metal for every transaction, which made trade much faster. Paper money came later still. It was first widely used in China around a thousand years ago, and European travellers were amazed that people would accept pieces of paper instead of gold. Today, money is changing again. In many countries, cash is disappearing as people pay with cards and phones, and some governments are experimenting with digital currencies. Yet the basic idea has hardly changed since the days of Uruk. Money only works because people trust that others will accept it. If that trust disappeared, a banknote would be nothing more than a piece of paper. In that sense, money is not really about metal or paper at all; it is about belief.

lines.s: Hi everyone, and welcome to Mind Lab. We all have habits we want to break and habits we want to build. To explain how it works, I'm joined by neuroscientist Dr Zaid Mahmoud.
Thanks for having me.
You often hear that it takes 21 days to form a habit. Is that true?

Unfortunately not. A well-known study from University College London found that it took participants 66 days on average for a new behaviour to become automatic, and for some people it took much longer.
66 days! That's depressing.
Not really. The good news is that missing one day didn't affect the process much. So if you slip up, don't give up.
How do habits actually work in the brain?

Think of a loop with three parts: a trigger, a routine and a reward. Your phone vibrates; that's the trigger. You check it; that's the routine. You get a little feeling of pleasure; that's the reward. The brain's reward system remembers that loop.
So how do we break a bad habit?
Change the environment. If you want to stop checking your phone in bed, leave it in another room. Make the bad habit harder and the good habit easier.

reading.text: In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel began a series of simple experiments at Stanford University. Children aged around four and five were taken into a room and offered a sweet, often a marshmallow. They were told that they could eat it immediately or, if they waited alone for about fifteen minutes, they would receive two. Some children ate the sweet the moment the researcher left. Others covered their eyes, sang songs or turned their chairs away to resist the temptation. Years later, Mischel's team contacted many of the original participants. They found that the children who had waited longer tended to have better exam results and other positive outcomes as teenagers. The study became famous as proof that deferred gratification, the ability to wait for a bigger reward, is a key to success. Had the story ended there, it would be a simple lesson about willpower. However, more recent research has complicated the picture. In 2018, a team repeated the experiment with a much larger and more varied group of children. The link between waiting and later success was much weaker, and it became weaker still once the researchers took into account factors such as family income and the mother's education. In other words, children from more stable homes may find it easier to wait, partly because experience has taught them that promises are kept. A child who has learnt that adults often break their word might reasonably decide that one sweet now is better than an uncertain two later. This does not mean that self-control is unimportant. It does suggest, however, that our behaviour is shaped not only by character but also by circumstances. Before we judge someone for being impulsive, it might be wise to ask what their environment has taught them.

lines.s: Welcome to Justice Today. Our question this week: what is prison actually for? I'm talking to criminologist Dr Huda Aziz. Huda, welcome.
Thank you. It's a question every society has to answer.
Most people would say prison is about punishment.
That's one purpose. But there are at least three others: protecting the public, acting as a deterrent, and rehabilitation, which means helping offenders return to society as law-abiding citizens.
Which one works best?

The evidence suggests that rehabilitation is the key to reducing crime. Norway is often given as an example. Its prisons focus on education and job training, and its rate of reoffending is thought to be among the lowest in the world.
But isn't that too soft on criminals?
That's a common reaction. But remember, almost all prisoners will be released one day. The question is: what kind of neighbour do you want them to be?
And what about short sentences for petty crimes?
Research suggests that community service is often more effective than short prison sentences for minor offences. It keeps people in their jobs and with their families, and it costs much less.

reading.text: For centuries, courts have treated eyewitness testimony as one of the most powerful forms of evidence. If someone stands up in court, points at the defendant and says, "That's the man I saw," juries tend to believe them. Yet psychologists have known for decades that human memory is far less reliable than we think. In a famous experiment in 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed students a film of a car accident and then asked them how fast the cars had been going. The only difference was a single verb in the question. Students who were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other gave much higher estimates than those who heard the word "hit". A week later, the "smashed" group was also more likely to report seeing broken glass, although there had been none in the film. Memory, it seems, is not like a video recording that we simply play back. Each time we remember an event, we rebuild it, and new information can change it without our noticing. Stress, poor lighting and the presence of a weapon can make things even worse. The consequences can be serious. In the United States, an organisation called the Innocence Project has helped to free hundreds of people who were wrongly convicted, many of whom had spent years behind bars. Mistaken eyewitness identification is reported to have played a role in around seven out of ten of these cases. As a result, many police forces have changed their procedures. Witnesses are now often told that the culprit may not be in a line-up, and the identification is carried out by officers who do not know the suspect, so that they cannot influence the witness, even accidentally. None of this means that witnesses are lying. They genuinely believe what they remember. That, in a way, is exactly what makes the problem so difficult.

lines.s: Welcome back. Today we're talking about something we all do but rarely think about: small talk. My guest is the linguist Dr Hadi Saleh. Hadi, welcome.
Thanks for having me.
Many people say small talk is a waste of time. Do you agree?
Not at all. When we chat about the weather or the traffic, we aren't really exchanging information. We're conveying a message: I'm friendly, and I'm safe to talk to.
So the words themselves don't matter much?
Exactly. In one study, people who chatted with a stranger on the train felt happier afterwards, even though they had expected to feel awkward.
Why do some people find it so hard, then?
Mostly fear. We worry about being tactless or running out of things to say. But you don't need perfect English to hold a conversation. Asking open questions is far more important.
Any tips for our listeners?
Start with something you can both see, ask "How about you?", and really listen. And remember, a slip of the tongue is not the end of the world!

reading.text: Every time an English speaker drinks coffee with sugar, studies algebra or reads a magazine, they are using words with Arabic roots. Linguists estimate that hundreds of English words came from Arabic, although most speakers are completely unaware of their etymology. The story began more than a thousand years ago. Between the eighth and thirteenth centuries, cities such as Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba were leading centres of science and learning. At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, scholars translated Greek texts into Arabic and added discoveries of their own. When European scholars later wanted to study mathematics, medicine and astronomy, they had to translate these Arabic books into Latin, and many technical terms simply passed into European languages. Mathematics provides the clearest examples. The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book by al-Khwarizmi, whose own name gave us the word algorithm. Zero and cipher both come from the Arabic sifr, and many stars, such as Aldebaran, still carry Arabic names. Trade was the other great route. Merchants carried goods, and the names of the goods travelled with them. Sugar, cotton, lemon and syrup all reached English through Arabic, often via Spanish, Italian or French. Even magazine comes from makhazin, meaning storehouses, and admiral comes from amir, meaning commander. Of course, words do not stay the same on such long journeys. Their sounds and meanings change, and some connotations disappear completely. Nobody buying a sofa today thinks of the raised platform, the suffa, that the word originally described. For Arab learners, this history offers a small but real advantage. English is not as foreign as it might first appear; hidden inside it are pieces of their own mother tongue.

lines.s: Why do so many prices end in 99? Marketing expert Layla Hassan is here to explain. Layla, welcome.
Thanks. It's called charm pricing, and it works surprisingly well.
But everyone knows 9.99 is basically 10!
We know it, but our brains read from left to right. We see the 9 first, so the price feels much lower. In one experiment, a dress sold better at 39 dollars than at 34.
Really? Even though it was more expensive?
Yes. Another trick is the decoy. Cinemas offer a small popcorn, a large one, and a medium one that is only slightly cheaper than the large. The medium exists to make you buy the large.
That sounds a bit manipulative.
Some people think so, but shops have to compete too. My advice is simple: before you buy, ask yourself whether you'd still want it at a round number.
So, if it says 99, think 100!
Exactly. And always read the small print.

reading.text: Ask people whether advertising affects them, and most will say no. They can see through slogans, ignore billboards and skip online ads after five seconds. Yet companies spend more than 700 billion dollars a year on advertising worldwide. Either businesses are wasting enormous amounts of money, or we are not as immune as we think. Research suggests the second explanation. One reason is the mere exposure effect: the more often we see something, the more we tend to like it, even if we never really pay attention to it. A jingle we have heard a hundred times while scrolling may feel strangely familiar when we see the product in a shop, and familiarity feels like trust. Advertisers also rarely try to convince us with facts. Instead, they connect products with feelings. A car advert shows freedom and open roads, not engine details; a soft drink is linked with friendship and summer. Over time, these associations are stored in memory, so the product becomes a shortcut to the emotion. Social media has made such techniques even more powerful. Platforms collect data about what we like, where we go and what we search for, which allows companies to target audiences with remarkable accuracy. An advert for running shoes may appear minutes after you mention a marathon in a message. Meanwhile, influencers present products as part of their daily lives, so it is often hard to tell where honest opinion ends and paid promotion begins. None of this means that we are helpless. Studies show that people who understand these techniques are less easily persuaded. Simply asking who paid for this, and what they want me to feel, can weaken an advert's power. Being a little cynical, in other words, may be one of the most useful consumer skills of the modern age.

lines.s: Welcome to Mind Lab. Today: discoveries that happened by accident. With me is science writer Nour Al-Amin. Nour, hello.
Hello! I love this topic, because it shows that science isn't always neat and planned.
Give us a famous example.

Penicillin, of course. In 1928, Alexander Fleming came back from holiday and noticed that mould had grown on one of his dishes, killing the bacteria around it. Most people would have thrown the dish away.
And the microwave oven?
That's another one. An engineer called Percy Spencer was working with radar equipment when he realised that the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted.
So is it all just luck?
Not at all. The French scientist Louis Pasteur said that chance favours the prepared mind. Fleming and Spencer noticed the anomaly because they knew exactly what normal looked like.
What's the lesson for the rest of us?
Pay attention to surprises. When something goes wrong, don't just fix it; ask why it happened. That's where discoveries hide.

reading.text: More than a thousand years ago, a scholar from Basra made a dangerous promise. According to a famous story, Ibn al-Haytham told al-Hakim, the ruler of Egypt, that he could control the floods of the Nile. When he travelled south and saw the size of the river, he realised that the plan was impossible. Fearing the ruler's anger, he is said to have pretended to be mad, and he spent years under house arrest in Cairo. It was during this period, according to tradition, that he wrote much of his greatest work, the Book of Optics. Before Ibn al-Haytham, many thinkers believed that we see because light comes out of our eyes and touches objects. He rejected this idea, arguing that vision happens when light reflected from objects enters the eye. What made his work remarkable, however, was not only his conclusion but the way in which he reached it. Instead of simply accepting the opinions of famous Greek writers, he designed experiments, many of which used dark rooms with a small hole in one wall. Light passing through the hole produced an upside-down image of the scene outside, a phenomenon now known as the camera obscura. Ibn al-Haytham insisted that a researcher should doubt everything, including his own ideas, and test every claim through observation and careful measurement. Results that could not be repeated, he believed, should not be trusted. This is very close to what we now call the scientific method, which is why some historians describe him as one of the first true scientists. His books were translated into Latin and influenced European scholars for centuries. Today, a crater on the Moon is named after him, and in 2015 UNESCO celebrated the International Year of Light partly in his honour. Not bad for a man who once had to pretend to be mad.

lines.s: Could you live without your smartphone for a month? Our guest, journalist Zainab Kareem, did exactly that. Zainab, welcome.
Thank you. It was one of the hardest things I've ever done!
Why did you decide to try it?
One evening I checked my screen time and saw that I'd spent almost seven hours on my phone. Seven hours! Feeling shocked, I bought a basic phone that could only make calls and send texts.
What was the hardest part?
The first week. I kept reaching into my pocket for a phone that wasn't there. And simple things became difficult, like finding an address without a map app.
Did anything get better?
Definitely. I slept better and read four books. Having nothing to scroll through, I actually talked to people on the bus!
Are you still using the basic phone?
No, I went back to a smartphone, but I deleted my social media apps and I never take it into the bedroom. Technology is a double-edged sword; you just have to decide who's in control.

reading.text: In 2018, a video appeared online in which a former American president seemed to insult his successor. It looked real and sounded real, yet he had never said those words. The video had been made by a film director and a news website to warn people about a new kind of technology: the deepfake. Deepfakes are videos, images or audio recordings created by artificial intelligence to show people doing or saying things they never did. Trained on thousands of photos and voice samples, machine-learning programs can copy a person's face, expressions and way of speaking with frightening accuracy. Only a few years ago, producing a convincing fake required expensive equipment and expert skills. Today, apps can generate one in minutes at the touch of a button. The technology is not always harmful. Film studios use it to make actors look younger, and one museum used it to bring back a famous painter who talks to visitors. Having lost their voices to illness, some patients have even had their voices recreated from old recordings. However, the risks are serious. Criminals have used cloned voices to phone employees, pretending to be their bosses and asking them to transfer money. Fake videos of politicians can spread misinformation before an election, and ordinary people have been targeted with fake images designed to humiliate them. Perhaps the greatest danger is more subtle: once people know that any video might be fake, they may stop believing real evidence too. So how can we protect ourselves? Experts are developing tools that detect tiny errors in fake videos, and some companies now add invisible watermarks to AI-generated content. But technology alone will not solve the problem. Before sharing a shocking video, it is worth asking where it came from and whether trusted media outlets have reported it. In the age of deepfakes, seeing should no longer mean believing.

lines.s: Is graffiti art or vandalism? Our guest today is street artist Mustafa Adel, whose murals cover walls in several Iraqi cities. Mustafa, welcome.
Thanks for inviting me.
Let's start with the big question. Is what you do art?
I think so, but it depends. If someone sprays their name on a wall without permission, that's vandalism. What I do is different: I ask the owner first, and I plan every design carefully.
How long does one mural take?
The big ones take about three weeks. The design alone can take longer than the painting.
What inspires you?
Mostly ordinary people. It was an old man selling tea near my house who inspired my first mural. I painted him smiling, with the river behind him.
How do people react?
Most are happy. Children stop to take selfies, and shop owners say more customers come. It's art that everyone can see for free, not just people who visit galleries.

reading.text: Deep inside a cave on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, there is a painting of a wild pig. It is red, simple and partly faded, and it is at least 45,000 years old, which makes it one of the oldest known pictures in the world. Whoever painted it had no museum to show it in and no buyer to sell it to. So why did they bother? This question has puzzled scientists for a long time. Making art takes time and energy, and it does not help us find food or escape danger, at least not directly. Yet every human culture that has ever been studied has produced some form of art, whether painting, music, dance or storytelling. One theory is that art helped early humans live together. Shared songs and images may have strengthened the bonds within a group, and groups that worked well together were more likely to survive. Another theory suggests that art was a way of showing off. Just as a peacock displays its tail, a skilled artist might have impressed others with talents that were hard to fake. More recent research focuses on the brain. Brain scans show that looking at a painting we find beautiful activates the same reward areas that respond to delicious food or good news. In other words, what art gives us is pleasure, and the brain is designed to seek pleasure out. Perhaps the most convincing answer, however, is that art allows us to share what is inside our heads. Language can describe a feeling, but a song or a painting can make someone else experience it. It is this ability to connect one mind to another that may explain why, 45,000 years later, a red pig on a cave wall still speaks to us.

lines.s: Imagine you find a wallet in the street. Would you return it? Psychologist Dr Samir Najjar is here to tell us about a famous experiment. Samir, welcome.
Thank you. In 2019, researchers handed in more than 17,000 wallets in 40 countries. They took them to hotels, banks and police stations, saying they'd found them on the street.
What was inside the wallets?
A key, a shopping list and business cards with an email address. Some wallets had no money, and some had about 13 dollars.
Let me guess: people kept the money.

That's what most experts predicted. But the opposite happened. Wallets with money were more likely to be returned than empty ones, and in some countries, wallets with even more money were returned most often.
Why would that be?
People don't want to see themselves as thieves. Keeping an empty wallet feels harmless, but keeping one with money feels like stealing. Our self-image matters more than we think.
So we're more honest than we believe?
In many ways, yes. It's time we gave people a little more credit.

reading.text: Imagine a runaway train racing down a track towards five workers who cannot escape. You are standing next to a lever. If you pull it, the train will switch to a side track, where it will kill one worker instead of five. Would you pull the lever? This is the famous trolley problem, first described by the British philosopher Philippa Foot in 1967. When people are asked this question, most say they would pull the lever. Saving five lives at the cost of one seems the logical choice. But now imagine a different version. This time, there is no lever. You are standing on a bridge above the track, next to a very large man. The only way to stop the train is to push him off the bridge onto the track. The result would be exactly the same: one person dies and five are saved. Yet most people say they would never push the man. It feels as if it were murder, even though the numbers have not changed. Why do we react so differently? Psychologists believe that two systems in our minds compete. One calculates results and asks which choice produces the best outcome. The other reacts emotionally to the idea of personally harming someone. Pulling a lever feels distant; pushing a person with your own hands feels deeply wrong. For a long time, the trolley problem was just a puzzle for philosophy students. Today, it has suddenly become practical. Engineers designing self-driving cars must decide what a car should do if an accident cannot be avoided. Should it protect its passengers at any cost, or should it choose the action that harms the fewest people? Supposing your car had to choose, which would you prefer it to save? There are no easy answers, but the question forces us to think about what we really believe is right.

lines.s: Today's guest has won three national debate championships. Lina Haddad, welcome to the show.
Thank you! I'm happy to be here.
What's the secret of a winning argument?
Structure. Judges want a clear claim, a reason and evidence. Not only do you need strong points, but you also need to explain why they matter.
And what about your opponents' arguments?

That's where most people go wrong. They ignore them. Never ignore the strongest counterargument; deal with it directly. If you concede a small point, judges see you as fair, which actually makes you more persuasive.
Interesting. What about nerves?
Everyone gets nervous. I prepare my first thirty seconds word for word, so I never freeze at the start. After that, I use short notes.
Any final tip?
Listen more than you speak. No sooner had I learned to listen properly than I started winning. You can only refute what you've understood.

reading.text: More than 2,300 years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle asked a question that every advertiser, lawyer and politician still asks today: what makes people change their minds? His answer, set out in his book Rhetoric, was that a speaker can persuade an audience in three ways, which he called ethos, pathos and logos. Ethos is about the speaker's character. We are more likely to believe people we trust, so a persuasive speaker first shows that they are honest, knowledgeable and on the audience's side. This is why doctors appear in adverts for toothpaste and why politicians talk about their humble beginnings. Rarely do we accept an argument from someone we consider dishonest, however logical it may be. Pathos is the appeal to emotion. A story about one sick child can move people more than statistics about thousands. Skilled speakers use vivid examples, powerful images and rhetorical questions to make the audience feel hope, anger or fear. Used responsibly, emotion makes an argument memorable; used dishonestly, it becomes manipulation. Logos is the appeal to reason: facts, evidence and clear logical steps. Not only does logos make an argument stronger, but it also protects it against attack, because a well-founded claim is much harder to refute than an emotional one. Aristotle believed that the best speakers combine all three. A speech with only logic may be correct but boring; one with only emotion may be exciting but empty. Modern research into communication largely supports his view. For students preparing for exams or debates, the lesson is simple. Before you speak or write, ask yourself three questions: Why should they trust me? What do I want them to feel? What evidence can I give them? Answer all three, and few arguments will be able to stand against yours.

lines.s: Today we're talking about one of the most special places in Iraq: the southern marshes. My guest is environmental engineer Ahmed Jassim from Nasiriyah. Ahmed, welcome.
Thank you. It's a subject very close to my heart.
For listeners who don't know, what makes the marshes so special?

They're among the largest wetlands in the Middle East. People have lived there for thousands of years, building houses from reeds and raising water buffalo. In 2016, they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
But they've had a difficult history.
Very. In the 1990s, they were drained, and by 2000 around ninety per cent had disappeared. After 2003, local people broke the dams, and a large part came back to life.
And today?

Today the biggest threat is water scarcity. Dams upstream, low rainfall and rising temperatures mean that less water reaches the south. In dry years, salinity rises and the buffalo struggle to survive.
Is there a ray of hope?
Yes. Better irrigation upstream could save huge amounts of water, and eco-tourism may well bring new income. But it's a race against time.

reading.en: The Hidden Life of a Plastic Bottle
reading.text: Every minute, around a million plastic bottles are bought somewhere in the world. Most of them are used for a few minutes and then thrown away, yet a single bottle is thought to take around 450 years to break down. In other words, a bottle used once at a wedding today may well outlive the grandchildren of everyone who attended. Plastic is not evil in itself. It is cheap, light and strong, and it has made modern medicine, transport and food storage possible. The problem is the way we use it. The world now produces around 400 million tonnes of plastic a year, and much of it is designed for single use. Only around nine per cent of all the plastic ever made has been recycled. The rest has been burned, buried in landfill or left in the environment. Much of this waste ends up in rivers and seas. In the water, plastic slowly breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which are eaten by fish and other animals. Scientists have now found microplastics almost everywhere they have looked: in Arctic ice, in table salt and even in human blood. The long-term effects on our health are still unclear, but few experts believe they are likely to be harmless. So what can be done? Recycling helps, but it is not enough on its own, because many types of plastic are difficult or expensive to recycle. Many governments are therefore trying to reduce plastic at the source, by banning single-use bags, taxing packaging or making companies responsible for collecting their own waste. Some of the most effective solutions are surprisingly old-fashioned: refillable bottles, glass jars and cloth bags. Individual choices matter too. Carrying a reusable bottle may seem like a tiny step, but if millions of people take it, the impact is bound to be significant.

lines.s: More than half of the world's population now lives in cities, and by 2050 it's expected to be nearly seventy per cent. Urban planner Dr Maryam Saeed joins us. Maryam, welcome.
Thanks. Yes, urbanisation is one of the biggest changes in human history.
Why are people moving to cities so quickly?
Mostly for jobs, education and healthcare. In many countries, water scarcity and poor harvests are also pushing farmers off the land.
What problems does that create?
When cities grow faster than their infrastructure, you get a housing shortage, traffic gridlock and pressure on the water supply. Many newcomers end up in informal areas without proper sanitation.
So are big cities a bad idea?
Not at all. Well-planned cities are actually more efficient. People travel shorter distances, share public transport and use less energy per person than in villages.
What makes a city well planned?
Mixed neighbourhoods where homes, shops and schools are close together, plenty of shade and green public space, and good public transport. A city should be designed for people, not just for cars.

reading.text: Imagine a city where everything you need every day is a fifteen-minute walk or bike ride from your front door: your school or workplace, a doctor, a bakery, a park and a place to meet friends. This is the idea behind the 15-minute city, a concept made popular by the French-Colombian professor Carlos Moreno and adopted by the mayor of Paris in 2020. For most of the twentieth century, cities were designed around the car. Planners separated homes from offices, shops and factories, and connected them with wide roads and motorways. The result, in many places, was sprawling suburbs, long journeys to work and streets that felt empty and unsafe after dark. People who could not drive, such as children, older people and those on low incomes, often found it hard to reach the services they needed. The 15-minute city turns this approach upside down. Instead of moving people across the city, it brings services closer to them. Empty car parks become playgrounds, ground-floor offices become cafés and clinics, and school yards are opened to families at weekends. In Paris, hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes have been created, and many streets near schools have been closed to cars. Supporters say the benefits are enormous: cleaner air, less noise pollution, healthier residents and a stronger community spirit. Critics, however, warn that the idea works best in dense, wealthy cities. In poorer neighbourhoods, it may be difficult to attract good shops and doctors, and improving an area can lead to gentrification, pushing local families out. For fast-growing cities in the Middle East, where summer heat can make walking difficult, the model would need to be adapted, with more shade, trees and covered walkways. Still, the central question it asks is a good one for any city: what would life be like if we designed streets for people rather than for cars?

lines.s: Weddings are one of the biggest events in any family. How have they changed in Iraq? Sociologist Dr Huda Kamal is with us. Huda, welcome.
Thank you. It's a lovely topic, and one that everybody has an opinion about!
What did weddings look like fifty years ago?

They were very communal. The whole neighbourhood helped: women cooked together for days, and the celebrations often took place in the street or in the family home. Admittedly, they were simpler, but they lasted much longer, sometimes a whole week.
And today?

Today most weddings take place in halls or hotels, and they're shorter. In other words, they're more private and more professional. Social media has also changed things; many couples now plan their wedding partly for the photos.
Is that a bad thing?
Not necessarily. However, costs have risen enormously, and many young men delay marriage because they can't afford it.
Which traditions have survived?
The henna night is still very popular, and so is the zaffa with its drums and music. After all, a wedding without a zaffa doesn't feel like a wedding to most Iraqis!

reading.text: Every culture has traditions that, if you think about them carefully, seem slightly strange. Why do we light candles on a birthday cake, or throw sweets over a bride and groom? Why do some families keep the same Friday lunch, at the same time, with the same dishes, for decades? From a purely practical point of view, many of these rituals achieve nothing. Nevertheless, people all over the world cling to them, and researchers have started to ask why. One answer is that traditions reduce anxiety. Psychologists have found that performing a ritual before a stressful event, such as an exam or a performance, can make people feel calmer and more in control. The ritual does not change the situation itself; however, it gives the mind a sense of order in an uncertain world. Traditions also bind groups together. When a family repeats the same celebration every year, it creates shared memories and a sense of belonging that connects grandparents with grandchildren. In other words, a tradition is a kind of message from one generation to the next: this is who we are. Admittedly, not all traditions deserve to survive. Some customs are expensive, while others may be unfair to particular members of the community. Cultures have always dropped some traditions and invented new ones, and this process is healthy. After all, many so-called ancient traditions are younger than we think; some were invented only a century or two ago. Globalisation has made this question more urgent. As young people watch the same films and use the same apps all over the world, many communities fear that their local customs will disappear. Yet the evidence suggests that traditions are surprisingly adaptable. Families now share Eid greetings on video calls, and young musicians mix traditional songs with modern beats. Traditions survive not by staying exactly the same, but by changing just enough to stay meaningful.

dialogue.en: From a Kitchen to a Brand
dialogue.ar: من مطبخ البيت إلى علامة تجارية

lines.s: Today's guest started a business in her mother's kitchen in Diyala and now sells to five countries. Noor Al-Tamimi, welcome!
Thank you! It still feels strange to hear it described like that.
How did it all start?
In 2019, I was a pharmacy student, and my mother made the best date syrup I'd ever tasted. I remember posting a photo of it on Instagram, and within an hour, twenty people had asked to buy some.
So you saw a gap in the market.
Exactly. Lots of people want traditional products but don't have time to make them. We started with fifty jars and a very tight budget.
What was the hardest part?
Cash flow, definitely. Customers paid late, but suppliers wanted their money immediately. We almost went under in the second year.
How did you survive?
We tried selling to cafés and bakeries instead of only to individuals. That gave us regular orders. Then we secured funding from a business incubator, which helped us scale up.
Any advice for young entrepreneurs?
Start small, but think big. And remember to listen to your customers; they'll tell you what to make next.

reading.text: Every year, millions of people around the world start their own business, and many of them dream of becoming the next great success story. The reality is less glamorous. Statistics vary, but studies suggest that about one in five new businesses fails within its first year, and around half have closed within five years. Why do so many promising ideas never get off the ground? The most common reason, according to analyses of failed startups, is surprisingly simple: there was no real market for the product. Founders often fall in love with their own idea and forget to check whether customers actually need it. They spend months building a perfect product, only to discover that nobody wants to pay for it. Successful entrepreneurs, in contrast, tend to test their ideas early with a simple version and listen carefully to feedback. The second major killer is money. Many businesses run out of cash before they become profitable, often because they grew too fast or underestimated their overheads. A company can be selling well and still go under if customers pay late while rent and salaries must be paid on time. This is why experienced investors say that cash flow matters more than profit in the early years. Other common problems include choosing the wrong team, pricing products badly and failing to adapt when the market changes. Interestingly, many famous companies only survived because they were willing to pivot. YouTube is said to have started as a video dating site, and Instagram began as a complicated check-in app before its founders noticed that users mostly enjoyed sharing photos. Failure, however, is not always a disaster. Many successful entrepreneurs failed several times before getting it right, and they remember those failures as their most valuable lessons. As one investor put it, the goal is not to avoid failure, but to fail cheaply, learn quickly and try again.

dialogue.en: The Woman Who Kept Her Seat

lines.s: On the first of December 1955, a woman in Montgomery, Alabama, refused to give up her seat on a bus. Historian Dr Faris Nouri tells us her story. Faris, welcome.
Thank you. Her name was Rosa Parks, and that small act changed American history.
Why did she have to give up her seat?

At that time, buses in the American South were segregated. Black passengers had to sit at the back, and if the bus was full, they were expected to stand for white passengers. When the driver told Rosa Parks to move, she simply said no.
People often say she was just tired after work.
That's a common misconception. She must have been tired, of course, but she was also an experienced activist. She later wrote that the only tired she was, was tired of giving in.
What happened next?

She was arrested, and the Black community decided to boycott the buses. For 381 days, thousands of people walked to work instead of taking the bus. The boycott was led by a young pastor called Martin Luther King.
And it worked?
Yes. In 1956, the US Supreme Court ruled that segregation on buses was illegal. It shows that ordinary people can change history when they take a stand together.

reading.text: In 2010, the United Nations officially recognised access to clean water and sanitation as a human right. It might seem strange that such a basic need had to be written down at all. Surely, you might think, everyone already agreed that people should be able to drink safe water. Yet more than two billion people around the world still lack safely managed drinking water, and hundreds of thousands of children die every year from diseases that clean water could prevent. Recognising water as a right changed the way governments and organisations talk about the problem. Water is no longer seen simply as a product that people buy, or as a service that only some areas deserve. Instead, governments have a duty to make sure that water is available, safe, affordable and physically accessible to everyone, including the poorest and most marginalised communities. In practice, however, rights on paper do not always become rights in reality. In many cities, wealthy districts enjoy a reliable water supply, while poorer areas on the edge of town depend on expensive water tankers. Women and girls are often the most affected, because in many societies they are responsible for collecting water, sometimes walking for hours each day. That time could have been spent at school or at work. Critics of past policies argue that some governments should have invested in water networks decades ago, instead of waiting for a crisis. Others point out that climate change and growing populations have made the challenge much harder than anyone could have predicted. For countries like Iraq, where the Tigris and Euphrates have shaped civilisation for thousands of years, the issue is especially urgent. Protecting the right to water will require better management, fair sharing between countries and communities, and a recognition that water is not just a resource, but the foundation of life and dignity.

dialogue.en: The Return of the Stolen Treasures

lines.s: In April 2003, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad was looted. Today, museum curator Dr Lina Al-Hashimi tells us what happened next. Lina, welcome.
Thank you. It's a painful story, but it's also a story of hope.
How many objects were stolen?
Around fifteen thousand. Some had been sitting in storerooms for decades, and many had never even been photographed, which made them very hard to trace.
How did you start to get them back?
Slowly. Some local people returned objects voluntarily, and police in other countries seized artefacts that had been smuggled abroad. Thousands of pieces were recovered within a few years.
Is there one return that stands out?

The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet. It's a small clay tablet with part of the Epic of Gilgamesh. It had been sitting in a museum in the United States, and in 2021 it finally came home. The same year, around seventeen thousand other artefacts were returned from the United States.
What's the lesson from all this?

reading.text: In the year 762, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur stood on the banks of the Tigris and chose the site for a new capital. According to the historian al-Tabari, the caliph had been looking for the perfect location for some time. He wanted a place with a good climate, easy access to the river for trade, and fertile land to feed a large population. The city he built, officially called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, would become one of the most famous cities in the world. Al-Mansur's design was unusual. Baghdad was built as a perfect circle, protected by two great walls and a deep moat. Four gates, facing different parts of the empire, led into the city, and at its centre stood the caliph's palace and the great mosque. Thousands of workers, architects and engineers had been brought from across the empire, and the Round City was completed in only about four years. The circle did not stay closed for long. As trade grew, markets and neighbourhoods spread far beyond the walls, and within a few decades Baghdad had become one of the largest cities on earth. In its heyday, it was home to scholars, poets, doctors and translators from many different backgrounds. At the House of Wisdom, they studied and translated works from Greek, Persian and Indian sources, and they made important advances in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Sadly, almost nothing of the original Round City survives today. Floods, wars and the Mongol conquest of 1258 destroyed much of medieval Baghdad, and later buildings were built on top of the ruins. Our knowledge of it comes mainly from historical records and the descriptions of travellers. Yet the city's legacy has stood the test of time. Its name still carries the memory of a golden age, when Baghdad was, for several centuries, the intellectual centre of the world.

dialogue.en: The Secrets of the Blue Zones

lines.s: Why do some people live to a hundred while others don't? Nutrition researcher Dr Karim Abbas has been studying the so-called Blue Zones. Karim, welcome.
Thank you. The Blue Zones are five regions where people live unusually long, healthy lives, places like Okinawa in Japan and Sardinia in Italy.
Do they all eat the same food?
Not exactly, but their diets have a lot in common. Each of these communities eats mainly plants: beans, vegetables, wholegrains and nuts. Meat is eaten, but usually only a few times a month.
Is it all about food?

Not at all. Neither diet nor exercise alone explains their longevity. These people move naturally every day, walking, gardening and cooking, rather than going to the gym. They also have strong family and social ties.
I've heard about a Japanese saying about food.
Yes. In Okinawa, older people say hara hachi bu, which means stop eating when you're about eighty per cent full. It's a simple way to avoid overeating.
What can our listeners do tomorrow?
Eat more beans and vegetables, walk whenever you can, and have dinner with people you love. None of these things are expensive, and all of them work.

reading.text: Ask people what they need to stay healthy, and most will mention a balanced diet and regular exercise. Far fewer will mention sleep. Yet scientists increasingly describe sleep as the third pillar of good health, just as important as food and physical activity. Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, and teenagers need even more. However, surveys suggest that a large proportion of people regularly get less than this. The causes are familiar: long working hours, late-night screens, caffeine, and the feeling that sleep is wasted time. In fact, the opposite is true. While we are asleep, the brain is extremely busy. One of its most important jobs is organising memory. During deep sleep, the brain replays the events of the day and moves important information into long-term storage. This is why students who sleep after studying usually remember more than those who stay up all night. Research on animals also suggests that sleep helps the brain clear away waste products that build up during the day, a little like a night-time cleaning service. The effects of sleep deprivation are serious. After about seventeen hours without sleep, people react as slowly as someone who has been drinking alcohol. In the long term, poor sleep has been linked to heart disease, weight gain and a weaker immune system. Every system in the body seems to suffer when sleep is cut short. The good news is that small changes can make a big difference. Experts recommend going to bed and getting up at the same time every day, even at weekends, to keep the circadian rhythm stable. Neither coffee nor heavy meals should be consumed late in the evening, and phones are best left outside the bedroom, because their light tells the brain that it is still daytime. Sleep, in other words, is not a luxury. It is one of the most powerful health tools we have, and it is completely free.

lines.s: Why do some of the world's best players miss penalties? Sports psychologist Dr Rasha Kadhim is here to explain. Rasha, welcome.
Thanks. Penalties are fascinating because they're more about the mind than the feet.
How often are penalties scored in a shoot-out?
Roughly three out of four. So the player taking it should feel confident. But when the pressure is colossal, even top players choke.
What do they do wrong?

Research shows that players who rush their kick, putting the ball down and shooting almost immediately, miss more often. Their nerves are controlling them. The calm ones take a breath and wait a second or two.
And goalkeepers?
That's interesting too. One study found that keepers dive left or right about ninety-four per cent of the time, even though staying in the middle would sometimes save more shots.
Why don't they stay in the middle?
Because if they stand still and the ball goes in, they look as if they did nothing. Diving feels better, even when it's worse! Psychologists call this action bias.
Any advice for young players?
Practise under pressure, choose your corner early, and take your time. Being in the zone is a skill you can train.

reading.text: How long does it take to become world-class at something? For years, the popular answer was 10,000 hours. The idea was made famous by the writer Malcolm Gladwell in his 2008 book Outliers, which was based partly on research by the psychologist Anders Ericsson. Ericsson had studied violin students in Berlin and found that the very best had practised far more than the others, an average of about 10,000 hours by the age of twenty. The message was absolutely thrilling for many people: talent is not a gift; it is simply the result of hard work. Practise for long enough, and you too could become a champion. Unfortunately, the reality is a little more complicated. Ericsson himself later complained that his research had been misunderstood. First, 10,000 was an average, not a magic number; some people became experts much faster, others much more slowly. Second, and more importantly, not all practice is equal. Hitting a thousand tennis balls without thinking is very different from what Ericsson called deliberate practice: working on specific weaknesses, with clear goals and immediate feedback, usually guided by a coach. Later studies have also shown that practice, although extremely important, does not explain everything. In sport, it seems to account for less than a fifth of the difference between athletes. Other factors, such as body type, the age at which you start, the quality of coaching and mental toughness, all play a part. So is the rule useless? Not at all. The research still sends a powerful message: very few people reach peak performance without years of focused effort. The difference is that the effort must be smart. As one coach put it, practice does not make perfect; perfect practice makes perfect.

lines.s: The oud is one of the oldest instruments in the world. Today we're talking to young oud player Yousif Amer from Baghdad. Yousif, welcome!
Thank you. It's an honour to talk about my favourite instrument.
How old is the oud, exactly?
Nobody knows for sure, but some of the oldest images of instruments like it come from Mesopotamia, from more than four thousand years ago. So you could say it was born here.
When did you start playing?

At nine. My grandfather played at family weddings, and I used to sit next to him and copy his fingers. Honestly, I nearly dropped out of my lessons at twelve, because it's a very difficult instrument and I wanted to play football instead!
What changed your mind?
I went to a concert by Naseer Shamma. The turnout was huge, and at the end the whole audience gave him a standing ovation. I thought, I want to do that one day.
Do young Iraqis still listen to the oud?
More than you'd think. A lot of young musicians mix the oud with electronic music or jazz, and those videos go viral. It's no longer only for older people.
Any advice for beginners?
Be patient. The first year is a letdown for most people, because it sounds terrible! But if you face up to that and keep practising, it becomes part of you.

reading.en: Why Do We Love Sad Songs?
reading.text: Every culture in the world seems to have sad songs. From Iraqi maqam to American blues, from lullabies to love songs about loss, people regularly choose music that makes them feel melancholy. At first glance, this is a strange habit. We usually try to avoid sadness in real life, so why do we put up with, and even seek out, sadness in music? Psychologists have come up with several explanations. One is that sad music allows us to feel emotions safely. When a song describes heartbreak, we experience a version of the feeling, but we know that nothing bad is actually happening to us. Some researchers suggest that the brain may even release chemicals that comfort us, as if we were really sad, which leaves us feeling calm and soothed rather than depressed. Another explanation is that sad songs make us feel less alone. In surveys, many listeners say that when they are going through a difficult time, a sad song feels like a friend who understands them. The lyrics put into words what they cannot express themselves, and this can be a great relief. In other words, the song does not create sadness; it shares it. Sad music is also strongly connected with memory. A melody from our teenage years can bring back a whole period of our life, with its people, places and feelings. This mixture of sadness and warmth, often called nostalgia, is one of the emotions people say they enjoy most in music. Interestingly, not everyone responds in the same way. People who score highly on empathy tend to enjoy sad music more, perhaps because they are more easily moved by other people's feelings. For them, a beautiful sad song is not a letdown but a kind of emotional gift. Perhaps this explains why, in Arabic, the word tarab describes not happiness or sadness, but the deep emotional state that great music produces in its listeners.

lines.s: Every year, people get lost in the desert, often just a few kilometres from a road. Survival instructor Mazin Hadi is here with some life-saving advice. Mazin, welcome.
Thank you. And yes, most desert emergencies start with a small mistake.
What's the most common one?
Leaving without telling anyone. Always tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back. That way, if something goes wrong, someone will raise the alarm.
Let's say your car breaks down. What should you do?
Stay with the car unless you can see help nearby. A car is much easier to spot from the air than a person, and it gives you shade.
What about water?

Take far more than you think you'll need, at least four litres per person per day in summer. And don't try to save it; drink it when you're thirsty. People have been found with water still in their bottles.
That's shocking. Is it safe to walk at night?
It's cooler, provided that you know exactly where you're going. Otherwise, you might walk in circles. If you're lost, it's usually better to stay put and make yourself visible.
Any final tip?
Respect the desert. It's beautiful, but it doesn't forgive mistakes. Take risks only if they're calculated risks.

reading.text: Every year, thousands of people pay large amounts of money to jump out of planes, climb frozen mountains or swim with sharks. Most of us would never do such things unless someone forced us. So why are some people so attracted to danger? Part of the answer lies in the brain. When we do something exciting, the brain releases dopamine, a chemical linked to pleasure and reward. Some people seem to need more of this excitement than others. Psychologists call this trait sensation seeking, and they have found that it varies a great deal from person to person. For high sensation seekers, a quiet life feels boring, while a calculated risk feels absolutely thrilling. Age matters too. Teenagers and young adults are famous for taking risks, and research suggests there is a biological reason. The parts of the brain that respond to reward develop earlier than the parts that control planning and self-control, which are not fully mature until the mid-twenties. In other words, the accelerator develops before the brakes. Interestingly, humans are often bad at judging risk. Many people are afraid of flying, even though, mile for mile, it is far safer than travelling by car. We tend to fear dramatic, rare events that appear in the news, while ignoring everyday dangers, such as driving while tired or not wearing a seatbelt. We also suffer from optimism bias: most of us believe that accidents happen to other people. None of this means that risk is always bad. Without people willing to take risks, there would be no explorers, no inventors and no new businesses. The key, experts say, is to take risks consciously. Ask yourself what the worst-case scenario would be, take sensible precautions, and go ahead only provided that the possible reward is worth it. Courage, after all, is not the absence of fear; it is acting wisely in spite of it.

lines.s: Have you ever gone to the supermarket for milk and come home with a full bag? Consumer psychologist Dr Zahra Mousa explains why. Zahra, welcome.
Thanks. Don't worry, it happens to almost everyone, and it's not entirely your fault.
So what's going on?
Well, think about where the milk and bread are. They tend to be at the back of the store, so you have to walk past hundreds of other products to reach them.
That's sneaky!

It's clever. Shelves are also carefully organised. The most profitable products are usually placed at eye level, while cheaper brands are often near the floor. There's a saying in the industry: eye level is buy level.
What about music?

One famous study found that when supermarkets played slow music, shoppers walked more slowly and spent more. The smell of fresh bread seems to have a similar effect; it makes us feel hungry and relaxed.
So how can we protect ourselves?
Make a list and stick to it, never shop when you're hungry, and look at the top and bottom shelves. To some extent, simply knowing about these tricks makes them less powerful.

reading.text: Imagine you are offered a choice between two chocolates: a luxury truffle for fifteen cents, or an ordinary chocolate for one cent. In a famous experiment by the behavioural economist Dan Ariely and his colleagues, most people chose the truffle, which seems a sensible decision; it was much better value. Then the researchers reduced both prices by one cent. The truffle now cost fourteen cents, and the ordinary chocolate was free. Logically, nothing important had changed, since the difference in price was exactly the same. Yet this time, most people chose the free chocolate. This result suggests that the word free has an unusually strong effect on the human mind. When something costs nothing, we tend to forget about its disadvantages and see only the benefits. A free product appears to carry no risk, and losing nothing feels extremely attractive. Arguably, this is why companies use the word so often: free delivery, free trials, buy one, get one free. However, free offers are rarely as generous as they seem. A free trial, for instance, often turns into a monthly payment that people forget to cancel. Free delivery may only apply if you spend more than a certain amount, which can lead customers to add items they did not plan to buy. In some cases, the free product is not really free at all; with many apps and websites, users pay with their personal data rather than with money. To some extent, understanding this effect can protect us. Before accepting a free offer, it may be worth asking a few simple questions: Would I want this if I had to pay for it? What will it cost me later? What am I giving away in return? None of this means that free offers are always bad. Sometimes a free sample genuinely helps us discover a product we love. But as the old saying goes, there is no such thing as a free lunch. Somebody, somewhere, usually pays.

lines.s: Imagine seeing a doctor without leaving your house. That's telemedicine, and our guest, Dr Omar Al-Jubouri, uses it every day. Omar, welcome.
Thank you. I'm a GP, and about a third of my appointments now happen by video.
Which patients benefit most?

People in remote villages, definitely. Some of my patients used to travel three hours to reach the nearest clinic. Now they can talk to me on their phone, and I can decide whether they really need to come in.
But surely you can't examine someone through a screen?
That's true, and it has limits. I can't listen to a patient's heart through a phone. But many things, like follow-up visits or checking test results, don't need a physical examination.
What about artificial intelligence?

It's already helping. Some programs can look at an X-ray and spot early signs of disease. By the time I see the image, the computer will already have highlighted anything unusual. But the final diagnosis must come from a human.
Where do you think all this is going?
By 2035, I think many routine check-ups will have moved online, at least partly. But medicine is about trust, and patients will always want a real person who listens.

reading.text: When Alexander Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in 1945 for his part in the discovery of penicillin, he gave a warning that sounds remarkably modern. If people used the new medicine carelessly, he said, bacteria would learn to resist it. Eighty years later, his warning has come true. Antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria change in ways that allow them to survive the medicines designed to kill them. Every time an antibiotic is used, most bacteria die, but a few with natural resistance may survive and multiply. Over time, these resistant bacteria become more common, and infections that were once easy to treat become dangerous again. The problem is made worse by the way antibiotics are used. In many countries, they can be bought without a prescription, and patients often take them for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses, not bacteria. Others stop taking their medicine as soon as they feel better, instead of finishing the full course. A large share of the world's antibiotics is also given to farm animals, often to make them grow faster rather than to treat disease. The consequences are already serious. A major study estimated that, in 2019, more than a million deaths around the world were directly caused by resistant infections. One British report warned that, by 2050, resistant infections could be killing as many as ten million people a year unless action is taken. Ordinary operations, such as a caesarean section or a hip replacement, could become risky once again. Fortunately, there are solutions. Scientists are developing new antibiotics and alternative treatments, and some countries have reduced their use of antibiotics in farming. Doctors are being trained to prescribe them only when they are truly necessary. But individuals have a role too. Only take antibiotics when a doctor says you need them, always finish the course, and never share them with others. By the time a new generation of medicines is ready, we will hopefully have learned to use them wisely.

lines.s: Today we're talking about the Arab world's journey into space. Astronomer Dr Huda Al-Rawi is with us. Huda, welcome.
Thank you. It's an exciting story, and it's moving faster than ever.
Who was the first Arab in space?
Prince Sultan bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, in 1985. He flew on an American space shuttle. Two years later, the Syrian pilot Muhammed Faris travelled to a Soviet space station.
And more recently?

The big moment came in 2021, when the UAE's Hope probe reached Mars. Then, in 2023, Sultan AlNeyadi spent six months on the International Space Station and became the first Arab to do a spacewalk. The same year, Rayyanah Barnawi became the first Saudi woman in space.
Why does this matter for young people in Iraq?

Because it shows that space isn't only for other countries. Our region has a long history in astronomy; many stars still have Arabic names. And some Iraqi engineers have already worked on small satellites.
What's next?
Several Arab countries are set to launch new missions, and some are on the verge of building their own rockets. I truly believe that an Arab astronaut will walk on the Moon within our lifetime.

reading.text: For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, Mars has fired our imagination. Today, the idea of living there no longer belongs only to science fiction. Several space agencies and private companies are working on plans to send people to the red planet, and a crewed mission is set to take place within the next few decades. But should we really try to live on Mars? Supporters argue that becoming a multi-planet species could protect humanity in the long term. If a disaster such as a giant asteroid ever destroyed life on Earth, a human colony elsewhere might allow our civilisation to survive. Others point out that space exploration has always produced unexpected benefits on Earth, from better water filters to medical equipment, and a Mars programme would be no exception. The challenges, however, are enormous. Mars is, on average, about 225 million kilometres from Earth, and a journey there would take around seven months. The planet's atmosphere is extremely thin and consists mainly of carbon dioxide, so nobody could breathe outside. Temperatures can fall below minus 100 degrees Celsius, and without a strong magnetic field, the surface receives dangerous levels of radiation. Any settlers would have to live in sealed buildings, grow food under artificial light and produce their own water and oxygen. There is also a moral question. Critics argue that the billions of dollars needed for a Mars colony would be better spent on solving problems on our own planet, such as climate change, poverty and disease. Some scientists add that, before we start changing another world, we should learn to look after the one we already have. Perhaps the most realistic answer lies somewhere in between. Small scientific bases on Mars may well be on the cards for this century, but a true city of millions is unlikely in the foreseeable future. Either way, the question forces us to think about what kind of future the human race really wants.

lines.s: Why do some teams achieve amazing things while others fall apart? Organisational psychologist Dr Saif Hamdan is here. Saif, welcome.
Thank you. It's the question every manager asks.
Is it about having the cleverest people?
Surprisingly, no. A few years ago, Google studied around 180 of its teams to find out what made the best ones different. They expected the answer to be intelligence or experience. It wasn't.
So what was it?
Something called psychological safety. In the best teams, people felt safe to ask questions, admit mistakes and share strange ideas without being laughed at.
How can a leader create that?

By listening, by admitting their own mistakes first, and by making sure everyone speaks in meetings, not just the loudest people. The research also found that people need to be dependable and to understand clearly what their role is.
What about conflict? Is it always bad?
Not at all. Healthy disagreement prevents groupthink. The problem is personal conflict. A good leader insists that people criticise ideas, not each other.
Any final tip?
Remember that a team isn't just a group of individuals. It's essential that everyone feel their work matters.
