reading.en: The Shepherd Who Leads from Behind
reading.text: In his autobiography, Nelson Mandela described a lesson he had learned as a boy from watching shepherds. A leader, he wrote, is like a shepherd who stays behind the flock, letting the most nimble go out ahead, while the others follow, not realising that they are being directed from behind. It is a surprising image of leadership, and it challenges the idea that leaders must always stand at the front, giving orders. Psychologists have been studying leadership styles for nearly a century. In a famous experiment in the 1930s, the psychologist Kurt Lewin and his colleagues placed groups of children in after-school clubs run by adults with different styles. Autocratic leaders made every decision themselves; democratic leaders involved the children in choices; and laissez-faire leaders gave almost no guidance at all. The democratic groups were generally the happiest and most creative. The autocratic groups often worked hard while the leader was watching, but they lost interest as soon as he left the room. The laissez-faire groups achieved the least. Modern research supports many of these findings. Teams usually perform best when leaders combine clear direction with real participation. Employees who feel listened to tend to be more committed, while those who are simply told what to do may do the minimum. This does not mean that a leader should never take control. In an emergency, a hospital or a fire brigade needs fast, decisive orders, and it is essential that everyone follow them immediately. Perhaps the best leaders are those who know which style a situation requires. Sometimes they lead from the front; at other times, like Mandela's shepherd, they step back and let others shine. As one writer put it, a boss says go, but a leader says let's go.

lines.s: Starting university can be exciting and terrifying at the same time. Dr Ruqaya Hussein, who teaches academic skills, joins us. Ruqaya, welcome.
Thank you. I meet hundreds of first-year students every year, and they all ask the same questions!
What's the biggest difference between school and university?

Independence. At school, teachers tell you exactly what to study. At university, you're expected to read widely, ask your own questions and manage your time. Nobody checks whether you've done the reading.
What about writing? Many students find academic essays difficult.

They do. The most common problem is that students describe instead of arguing. A good essay doesn't just say what other people think; it uses evidence to support a clear position. And every idea from another writer needs a citation.
That brings us to plagiarism.

Yes. Many students don't plagiarise deliberately; they just don't know how to paraphrase or cite sources properly. My advice is simple: when you take notes, always write down where the information came from.
And how should students deal with deadlines?
Start early and break big tasks into small steps. Writing a few hundred words a day is much easier than cramming the night before. And proofread everything; small mistakes can cost you marks.

reading.text: Academic writing has a reputation for being difficult to read, and sometimes the reputation is deserved. Long sentences, unfamiliar vocabulary and heavy use of nouns can make a research article feel like a wall of words. Yet the features that make academic English challenging are not usually there by accident. Each of them serves a purpose. Consider nominalisation, the habit of turning actions into nouns. Instead of writing that scientists measured the temperature and found that it had increased, a researcher might write that measurement revealed a significant increase in temperature. The second version is shorter, more objective and easier to connect to the next idea. In other words, nouns allow writers to pack complex processes into compact phrases, which can then become the subject of further argument. Hedging is another key feature. Careful researchers rarely claim to have proved something absolutely. They write that results suggest, indicate or appear to show, because scientific knowledge is always open to revision. The passive voice, meanwhile, keeps the focus on the research rather than on the researcher: the fact that the samples were analysed matters more than who analysed them. It is worth remembering that science has not always been written in English. During the golden age of Baghdad, Arabic was the language in which much of the world's science, medicine and mathematics was written, and for centuries afterwards Latin was the international language of European scholarship. Today, English plays this role, albeit with growing criticism that it disadvantages researchers who are not native speakers. Recently, many scientists have also argued that academic writing has become unnecessarily complicated. Clarity, they insist, is a sign of intelligence, not a lack of it. The best academic writers, therefore, combine precision with simplicity: they use formal structures where they help, but they never hide a simple idea behind complicated words.

lines.s: For our final episode, we're talking about fluency. Dr Leila Mansour speaks six languages and teaches language learning at university. Leila, welcome.
Thank you. It's a pleasure to be part of the final episode!
Let's start with the big question. Is there a secret to becoming fluent?
If there is one, it's this: speak before you feel ready. Most learners wait until their English is perfect, but fluency comes from speaking, not the other way round.
But what about mistakes?

Mistakes are part of the process. Native speakers make them too! The important thing is to be intelligible. Nobody will remember a small grammar mistake, but they will remember whether you communicated your idea.
Many listeners say they reach a plateau. They study for months and feel no progress.

That's completely normal. Your brain is still learning, even when you can't see it. Change something: read a different kind of book, watch films without subtitles or start keeping a journal. And look back at where you were a year ago; you'll be surprised.
Any final advice for people who've just finished a B2 course?

Don't stop! B2 is a fantastic achievement, but it's a door, not a wall. Find something you love doing, whether it's football, cooking or science, and do it in English every day. That's how a language stops being a subject and becomes part of who you are.

reading.en: How the Brain Learns a Language
reading.text: When you learned your first language, you did not study grammar rules or memorise word lists. You simply listened, copied and played, and by the age of five you could speak with remarkable fluency. Learning a second language as a teenager or an adult feels very different, and many people conclude that their brains are simply too old. The evidence, however, tells a more encouraging story. It is true that young children have certain advantages, particularly with pronunciation. Children who grow up with a language usually develop a native-like accent, whereas adults often keep traces of their first language. But adults have strengths too. They can understand grammar explanations, use dictionaries, set goals and reflect on their own learning, a skill psychologists call metacognition. Several studies have found that, in the early stages, older learners actually make faster progress than young children. What matters most is not age but how the brain is used. Memory research shows that we remember information far better when we have to retrieve it, so testing yourself is much more effective than simply rereading notes. Spacing your reviews over days and weeks, rather than cramming them into one evening, also makes new words last. This is why the review plan in this book asks you to return to each day after one, three, seven, fourteen and thirty days. Emotion plays a role as well. The brain gives priority to information that feels meaningful, so words connected to your own life, interests and experiences are easier to remember than isolated lists. Sleep is essential too; while you rest, the brain organises what you learned during the day. Finally, it is worth remembering that fluency is not a finish line. Even native speakers keep learning new words throughout their lives. Having reached B2, you have not finished learning English; you have simply become the kind of learner who knows how to keep going.
